title: China's Irrigation‐Induced Evapotranspiration Largely Returns to Land as Precipitation Through Atmospheric Recycling
content:
Abstract

Irrigation-induced evapotranspiration (IrrET), the atmospheric flux of irrigation water consumption (IWC), is commonly treated as local freshwater depletion, yet where this water returns as precipitation through atmospheric recycling remains poorly quantified. Here, we develop a high-resolution estimate of China's IrrET and combine it with Lagrangian moisture tracking to quantify its contribution to local and remote precipitation. This approach identifies where water vapor originating from IrrET contributes to precipitation, rather than simulating the dynamical precipitation response to irrigation. IrrET was estimated from the residual between satellite-based evapotranspiration and ERA5-Land baseline evapotranspiration, while accounting for inter-dataset biases and irrigated cropland fraction. The resulting IrrET estimates showed strong agreement with prefecture-level IWC statistics after calibration (R = 0.91, Rbias = −6%, root mean square error = 0.28 km3 yr−1). During 2008–2017, China's IrrET contributed 189.5 km3 yr−1 to precipitation, of which 65% fell over land, including 47% within China and 18% over neighboring terrestrial regions. Moisture tracking further revealed contrasting regional source–sink relationships, with the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and Loess Plateau receiving net atmospheric water inputs, whereas the remaining zones acted as net atmospheric water exporters. China's IrrET increased at a rate of 2.8 km3 yr−2 during 2000–2020, mainly due to irrigated-area expansion. This increase was associated with an additional 73.6 km3 of attributed precipitation under fixed climatological source–sink relationships. These results link local irrigation water depletion with regional moisture recycling and show that atmospheric redistribution should be considered when assessing irrigation sustainability in coupled human–water–climate systems.
